text: The crawler finished and created a table. But before trusting it, it's worth actually reading what the crawler inferred — because schema inference isn't magic, and it doesn't always get every column exactly right.

Checking the table definition shows six of seven columns came back correctly — order_id and quantity as bigint, unit_price as double, product_category, product_name, and customer_region all as string. One column is worth stopping on: order_date came back as a plain string, when it really holds date values.

Here's why. CSV files carry no built-in type information — every value is just text until something decides otherwise. The crawler's classifier samples values like 2026-08-01 and has to guess. In this case it played it safe and called the whole column a string rather than risk guessing a date format wrong and making values unreadable. That's a reasonable default, not a bug to panic over.

There are two real ways to fix this. The first is casting at query time, right inside Athena, using date_parse to convert the string into a usable date — no schema change required. That's the lowest-effort fix, and since there's no repeated job depending on this table, it's exactly the right fit here.

The second option is editing the Glue Catalog's column type directly, so every future query sees order_date as a real date without needing to cast it. That's the right call once a table is load-bearing — relied on repeatedly by other jobs or dashboards — which is exactly the situation the Intermediate project's curated dataset will be in later.
With the schema understood, and one known quirk accounted for, next lesson runs the first real SQL query against this table in Athena — proving the whole pipeline actually works end to end.
